data.title: Middle East Eye: India clears Israeli firm Cellebrite to supply phone-hacking tools to government agencies
data.author: Mee User
data.summary:
India clears Israeli firm Cellebrite to supply phone-hacking tools to government agencies
India has exempted Israeli surveillance company Cellebrite from domestic procurement rules, allowing government agencies to purchase its phone-extraction and hacking technology, an investigation has found.
The digital-rights group Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found that Home Minister Amit Shah approved a waiver for the National Investigation Agency (NIA), clearing the way for the purchase of at least 422 foreign forensic products, including Cellebrite tools.
The technology can extract data from seized devices and use recovered login tokens to access more than 100 cloud services, including social media platforms such as Instagram, X and Tinder.
Digital-rights experts have warned that the expansion of surveillance capabilities raises serious privacy concerns, with India's existing laws offering inadequate safeguards against excessive monitoring.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing
data.author: Amina Shareef
data.summary:
Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing
Submitted by
Amina Shareef
on

The ongoing genocide in Palestine is among the most devastating expressions of a global Islamophobic logic centred on the 'terrorist' figure
Civilians watch as health ministry workers bury the bodies of unidentified Palestinians at a mass grave in southern Gaza, on 30 January 2024 (Mohammed Abed/AFP)
Off
Hospitals, schools and residential buildings have been bombed. Water and sanitation infrastructure have been destroyed, amid warnings of mass malnutrition and starvation.
No, these are not headlines from Gaza - although they could be. They are from Iran and Lebanon, two countries that have been systematically targeted by the Israeli military over the past three years.
Yet the destruction of civilian life in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran is not an isolated phenomenon. Across different political contexts, Muslim and Muslim-adjacent populations have long been subjected to violence, abandonment and containment.
Well before 2023, hundreds of civilians were killed by US drone warfare in Yemen; refugees attempting to reach Europe were abandoned to death in the Mediterranean by the EU; and millions of displaced Syrians were warehoused in camps enclosed with barbed wire.
What connects these, and countless other cases, is the discourse of terrorism. It does not simply identify populations as security threats; it justifies managing those threats through lethal means. Death is administered immediately or slowly, by creating conditions that expose people to premature death.
These interconnected practices of death-dealing across multiple geographical sites reveal the global operations of anti-Muslim racism.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation
data.author: Mee User
data.summary:
Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation
Toyota has said it is investigating the use of its forklifts by the Israeli military after Middle East Eye found photos and videos of the vehicles at weapons and munitions storage sites, serving supply lines for frontline units, and being used by the army’s Logistics Corps.
It comes after MEE uncovered details of a previously unreported 158m-shekel ($49.8m) contract between Toyota and Israel’s Ministry of Defense for the supply of forklifts that was signed in 2024 – the first full year of the Gaza war.
Toyota says that its vehicles are not intended for military use.
When asked about the contract, the company told MEE it had commitments in place with both the defence ministry and its official reseller in Israel to ensure that its technology and products were “for civil use only”.
But when MEE then shared footage posted on official Israeli military social media channels, which showed Toyota forklifts being used at locations including a missiles and ammunition depot in northern Israel, a Logistics Corps training base, and inside a munitions factory, it said it was investigating the images to determine whether those agreements had been breached.

A prominent rabbi in Israel has invoked a Jewish religious doctrine permitting the use of lethal force against politicians who cooperate with Arab parties, Haaretz reported.
Rabbi Gedalya Axelrod, a former head of the Haifa Rabbinical Court, said in a handwritten ruling that Jewish party leaders who support a government formed with the backing of Arab parties are subject to din rodef, or the “law of the pursuer”.

Under Jewish religious law, a rodef is someone who poses a threat to another person's life and may be stopped by any means necessary. The doctrine was invoked by Yitzhak Rabin’s assassin, Yigal Amir, to justify the prime minister’s killing in 1995.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel extends $3,500 departure grant to nationals of all African countries
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Israel extends $3,500 departure grant to nationals of all African countries
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 11:39
Officials hope payment will bring number of departure back up after resettlement routes to Canada and the United States narrowed
In this file photo, residents of the southern district of the Israeli city of Tel Aviv protest against the presence of African refugees and asylum seekers on 30 August 2018 (AFP)
Off
Israel is extending its $3,500 voluntary departure grant to nationals of every African country in a bid to reverse a decline in the number of migrants leaving with state assistance, according to Haaretz.
Until now the payment had been limited mainly to people from a handful of states.
The change took effect on Monday and will remain in place until the end of the year, Israel's Population and Immigration Authority said. Applications must be submitted by 31 December.
It covers African nationals who have stayed in Israel for more than two years without a valid visa, and those holding temporary residency permits.
For the first time, it also includes people who entered Israel legally but overstayed their visas.
The authority expects several thousand more people to be eligible, including citizens of Nigeria, South Africa and Togo.
Before the change, the grant was mostly open to people who crossed into Israel outside official border points. That group includes nationals of Eritrea, Sudan, Ethiopia, Ivory Coast and Guinea, along with citizens of countries that have no diplomatic relations with Israel.
The authority’s figures show that 3,511 African nationals left with help from its Voluntary Departure Unit in 2024. That fell to 2,815 in 2025, a drop of about 20 percent.
In its 2025 annual report, the authority blamed smaller asylum quotas in Canada, the closure of US borders to asylum seekers, and war-related airspace closures that disrupted flights.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Art against erasure: A Palestinian sculptor and a Lebanese painter on war, exile and memory
data.author: Victoria Brittain
data.summary:
Art against erasure: A Palestinian sculptor and a Lebanese painter on war, exile and memory
Submitted by
Victoria Brittain
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 12:11
Abdul Rahman Katanani and Ayman Baalbaki, close as brothers, have spent decades turning the violence of their youth into work shown in museums and collections worldwide
Abdul Rahman Katanani in his studio outside Beirut (Victoria Brittain/MEE)
Off
The large studios of Abdul Rahman Katanani and Ayman Baalbaki are filled with canvases and installations about memory and destruction, drawn from the Israeli wars that shaped both artists’ youth.
These magical spaces, one in an anonymous building in busy central Beirut, and the other far from the city in a village high in the hills, speak for Lebanon and Palestine.
They also define the two artists and their families.
Katanani’s materials are barbed wire, corrugated metal sheets, olive branches, petroleum barrels and discarded clothes from his birthplace, the Sabra and Shatila refugee camp.
“I’ve always wanted to use the materials of the camp. These materials are our shadows. No... they’re us,” he told Middle East Eye.
The harsh materials yield startling lyrical shapes, such as a nine-metre wave in barbed wire, a child playing, a lotus flower and a bright early collage of clothes, including the unexpectedly intimate detail of underwear.
Once, he built a replica of the Palestinian camp of his childhood, shown inside an art gallery.
Ayman Baalbaki in his studio (Victoria Brittain/MEE)
Baalbaki’s very large mixed-media paintings are distinctive. They feature multiple thick layers of paint, often acrylic, in both intense and subtle colours. Many form part of a mesmerising series.
One such series, Destruction and Loss , depicts the ruin of Beirut’s iconic buildings, like his 2015-16 iconic painting of the Barakat Building on the corner of Damascus Road on the Green Line of the 15-year-long civil war.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UAE remains ‘main destination’ for gold smuggled out of Sudan and other war zones
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
UAE remains ‘main destination’ for gold smuggled out of Sudan and other war zones
Submitted by
Oscar Rickett
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 14:04
United Arab Emirates 'imported at least 591 tonnes of illicit gold into the country in 2024', new report from Swissaid finds
Bars of gold in a shop in the Dubai Gold Souk on 13 April 2026 (Fadel Senna/AFP)
Off
The United Arab Emirates remains the key trading hub for smuggled gold and conflict gold, a new report from Switzerland’s Swissaid foundation has found.
Despite the introduction in 2023 of legislation intended to curb illegal flows, the UAE, which is now the world’s second largest gold trading hub after Switzerland, imported at least 591 tonnes of illicit gold into the country in 2024.
Illicit gold refers to that which was either smuggled to the UAE - most often to the gold markets of Dubai, the second largest Emirate - without being able to be traced, or that comes from countries at war, including Yemen, Sudan and Russia.
The UAE remains by far the main destination for gold linked to armed conflicts in Africa, according to Swissaid. It also continues to be a major destination for gold exports from countries subject to international sanctions.
“The findings of this study are deeply concerning. They show that the United Arab Emirates remains a hub for smuggled and conflict gold,” said Marc Ummel, head of Swissaid’s commodities unit and co-author of the study.
In 2024, the UAE imported at least 174.5 tonnes of gold from Russia (directly and indirectly via Armenia), Yemen and Sudan (directly and indirectly), Swissaid found. The entire volume from these three countries can, the organisation said, “be considered as conflict gold”.
Gold and war
The UAE has been directly involved in both the wars in Yemen and Sudan, where it is the patron of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group widely determined to have committed genocide in different parts of Darfur.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Senior Chabad rabbi condones killing Jewish politicians who work with Arabs
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Senior Chabad rabbi condones killing Jewish politicians who work with Arabs
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 14:22
Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidic movement distances itself from Gedalia Axelrod's 'personal opinion'
Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod (YouTube screengrab)
Off
A senior Chabad rabbi has been criticised by his own movement after he said it was permissible to kill Jewish Israeli politicians who worked with Arabs.
Gedalia Axelrod, a senior cleric in the Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidic movement, issued a halakhic ruling earlier this week in which he said that Jewish politicians who form a government backed by Palestinian citizens of Israel were "din rodef", which roughly translates as "law of the pursuer".
Under Jewish religious law, a rodef is someone who poses a threat to another person's life and may be stopped by any means necessary.
The doctrine was previously invoked by Yitzhak Rabin’s assassin, Yigal Amir, to justify the prime minister’s killing in 1995.
Axelrod wrote that collaboration with Arab parties "poses a terrible danger to the people of Israel in the Holy Land and around the world".
Collaboration could either take the form of inviting Arab parties to join a governing coalition, or even relying on their support from outside it.
Swift condemnation
Axelrod's comments were swiftly condemned by the leadership of his religious movement, with Chabad spokesperson Rabbi Shimi Segal clarifying that his statements did not represent the official Chabad position.

data.author: Mee User

Palestinian rights group says Israel barred its director from travelling abroad
Israel barred Shawan Jabarin, the general director of Palestinian human rights group Al-Haq, from travelling to Jordan after stopping him at the Allenby Bridge crossing on Friday, the organisation said.
In a statement, Al-Haq said Israeli forces questioned Jabarin about the purpose of his journey before informing him that he was banned from travelling.
The organisation said the restriction were politically motivated and linked to his human rights advocacy.
Al-Haq said Jabarin had previously faced travel restrictions and threats over his work. It cited a 2022 warning call from Israel’s Shin Bet and said a travel ban imposed in 2006 remained in force for six years before being temporarily lifted in 2012.
The organisation said he had also been prevented from travelling to the Netherlands in 2009 to receive a human rights award.

Raqiq’s father Ahmed, stood weeping outside Nasser Hospital, as he held his son’s shrouded body.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Turkey and Qatar sign mutual defence agreement
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Turkey and Qatar sign mutual defence agreement
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 15:49
Announcement by Turkish presidency is the latest in a series of defence agreements amongst Middle Eastern and Islamic states
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan pictured with Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani during a welcoming ceremony at the presidential complex in Ankara, 8 August 2024 (Murat Cetin Muhurdar/Turkish presidential press office/AFP)
Off
Turkey and Qatar have signed a mutual defence agreement in Istanbul on Friday, in what is the latest military pact between Ankara and other Muslim states.
The defence agreement was one of five agreed between Turkey and Qatar, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
A statement by the Turkish president's office said that Friday's mutual defence agreement with Qatar "would add another dimension to our brotherhood".
Erdogan said Turkey and Qatar’s cooperation in the defence industry would continue to grow, according to the statement.
Turkey and Qatar have had several defence agrements since 2017, including the hosting of Turkish troops in Doha, but the new deal obliged both countries to come to the other's defence.
In August this year, Turkey signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, known as the Mecca Agreement.
Last week, the Turkish parliament passed a law approving the Mecca defence pact early on Friday, completing a crucial stage in the legal process.
The move will allow the deployment of Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia, which is currently at war with Yemen's Houthis.
In October, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that any deployment to Saudi Arabia would be defensive in nature and that Turkish forces would not operate in Yemen.
